A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same adaptive MMD-based personalized federated learning work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on CIFAR-10, Synthetic, Fed-ISIC2019, and RxRx1, including performance results in Tables 1–2 and ablations in Figures 2–3.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original MR-MTL experiments in Appendix F, Table 4.

M1.justification: Appendix F introduces an implemented MR-MTL adaptation using the MMD penalties. Unlike Ditto, it constrains local models against their aggregate without separately training global models. The original Ditto algorithm, MMD objectives, and kernel-update procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same CIFAR-10 heterogeneity settings, two Synthetic settings, Fed-ISIC2019, and 50-class, three-channel RxRx1. The new MR-MTL experiments reuse this coverage without introducing another task, population, or input scenario.

E2.justification: Previously cited but unevaluated MR-MTL becomes a baseline for its MK-MMD20 and MMD-D extensions in Table 4. Existing comparators are retained. Table 1 also displays Ditto directly using scores already reported in v1 Table 2.

E3.justification: Appendix F adds MR-MTL-specific hyperparameter searches while retaining the existing models, training schedules, and checkpointing. Appendix B.4 changes the stated RxRx1 learning rate from 0.001 to 0.0001, matching Table 3 in both versions. This corrects the reported setting without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The penalty-weight sensitivity, constraint-depth ablation, and optimized-versus-fixed-kernel analyses retain identical plotted results in Figures 2–3. The MR-MTL appendix adds benchmark comparisons, without a new ablation, robustness test, or error analysis.

E5.justification: v1 reports three-run means without dispersion. v2 newly supplies standard deviations for the principal Ditto/MMD comparisons in Table 6 and the MR-MTL results in Table 4. The original three runs and seeds remain unchanged, with seed information moved to Appendix B; no significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Table 4 adds MR-MTL and extension results across all seven dataset settings. For example, RxRx1 accuracy is 64.065 for MR-MTL versus 66.673 with MMD-D, whereas Fed-ISIC2019 decreases from 70.628 to 70.366. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores. Original accuracy means in Tables 1–2 and plotted results in Figures 2–3 are unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 adds asymptotic runtime derivations for Ditto and both MMD extensions, assuming one constrained layer and kernel optimization every local step. Existing mathematical definitions and objectives remain unchanged. Appendix H sketches a possible theoretical setting but supplies no new convergence or optimality proof.

C1.justification: The stated contribution now explicitly includes adapting MR-MTL alongside Ditto, and the introduction specifies cross-silo pFL as the target setting. The central claim that adaptive latent-space constraints help particularly under feature heterogeneity is retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of why Synthetic data can disadvantage weight penalties, why feature and weight constraints may complement each other, and why constraining additional layers may hinder learning. Section 5.1 and Appendices D–H expand communication, privacy, computational, applicability, and theoretical limitations, including the MR-MTL failure on Fed-ISIC2019. Several mechanism explanations are explicitly conjectural.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly identifies the qpth solver and the deep-kernel network's four linear layers with hidden dimension 50. Appendix F and Table 5 document MR-MTL tuning and selected hyperparameters. The under-five-minute Synthetic runtime statement changes from data generation to training all methods. The code-access link and existing hardware disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive comparisons with FedProto and earlier fixed-MMD FL methods, including FedMMD. New Appendix E positions the approach relative to split-model methods and other pFL families, including FedPer, FedRep, APFL, FedBN, HypCluster, and FedPop. This substantially expands novelty and applicability positioning.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work narrative are revised, explanations are clarified, and the existing constraint-interaction discussion receives its own subsection. The title expands FL to Federated Learning, and author information changes. The main section sequence and much existing prose remain intact; most added length documents new substantive content.

P2.justification: New Tables 4–6 present MR-MTL results, its hyperparameters, and a consolidated uncertainty display for the original results. Table 1 gains a Ditto column and revised ranking emphasis. Figures 1–3 retain their visual content, with placement, sizing, and caption adjustments.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens two weaknesses of v1: transfer beyond Ditto was untested, and principal comparisons lacked uncertainty reporting. MR-MTL experiments, including negative findings, and standard deviations make the evidence more informative, while implementation disclosures and closer prior-work comparisons improve reproducibility and positioning. The new complexity analysis is internally inconsistent about latent-space versus kernel-weight dimensions, but this localized flaw does not outweigh the empirical and reporting gains.
